On the first and last nights, when the group is together in a San Jose hotel, students room with same-gender peers with staff in adjacent rooms. Both Sundays and one Saturday belong entirely to the host family with no Rustic Pathways programming. Max 16 students, placed two per household.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Spanish Language Immersion in Costa Rica program page, Supervision & Safety and Program Details FAQ sections

dayToDay.notes: Students live with a Spanish host family in Siguenza, two Rustic Pathways students per household (or three on request), on full board, for two weeks -- sleeping at the host family's house rather than with the group. An alternative group-house option (El Albergue, an 18th-century house in the medieval centre) exists for students not ready for a homestay, where they instead room with same-gender peers. Program Leaders are based locally in Siguenza for the whole program, see every student at the school each weekday, and are reachable at any hour. Host families are long-standing partners of Segontiae Hispanic Studies rather than a rotating list. Both Saturdays have no Rustic Pathways programming at all and belong entirely to the host family. Max 20 students, placed two (or three on request) per household.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Spain: Spanish Language Immersion program page, Supervision & Safety and Group & Logistics FAQ sections

dayToDay.notes: Students share rooms with same-gender peers in a single Seoul guest house within reach of the language school in Hongdae, with both of the program's two Program Leaders staying in the same building throughout. This is the smallest group on any Rustic Pathways program researched: max 6 students with 2 dedicated Program Leaders, well below the org-wide 7:1 ceiling. Students get structured free time in pairs or threes with leaders reachable and a set meeting point; there is no unsupervised time outside agreed areas.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Korean Language Immersion in Seoul program page, Supervision & Safety and Group & Logistics FAQ sections

dayToDay.notes: 11 nights coastal campground in Sardinia, shared tents (2-3/tent, gender-organized), 2 nights Airbnb-style group house in Rome. Flush toilets, showers every 1-2 days. Students share camp setup/breakdown and chores. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Italy: Dive the Med, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Mix of local guesthouses, traditional riads, one desert-camp night, gender-divided rooms (2-5 students). Daily showers. Students help with daily tasks like tidying. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Morocco: Desert Nights, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Tent camping Pacific Coast to Sierra Nevada, 2 nights hostel at start. Showers every 3-4 days. Everyone helps set up camp, cook, clean. Serves grades 6-8. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, California: Pacific Sun, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Three accommodation types: tent camping (showers every 2-3 days), 1 night mountain refuge during multi-day hike, 5 nights private group house in rural Italy. Group helps set up tents, cook, care for shared spaces. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, France & Italy: Alps Adventure, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Tent camping in/near Acadia National Park all week, both MS and HS sessions. Flush bathrooms, short showers (no frequency given). Group sets up camp, cooks, keeps spaces clean together. No staff ratio stated; families of MS students should confirm added supervision for the younger band.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Maine: Pathway to the Pines, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Tent camping on Maui for the full two weeks at a beachside campground, shared tents (2-3/tent, gender-divided). Flush toilets, showers, and laundry facilities on-site. Showers every 1-2 days. Everyone pitches in to set up camp, cook, and keep shared spaces clean. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Hawaii: Island Exploration, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Tent camping for most of the trip (front-country to remote backcountry sites, shared tents 2-3/tent, gender-divided), plus 2 nights in family-friendly hostels in Oslo and Bergen (private rooms, 2-4 people, gender-divided). Most campsites have basic bathroom access; backcountry uses portable or natural setups. Showers every 2-4 days. Group pitches tents, preps meals, maintains camp together. No staff ratio stated. Likely more physically demanding day-to-day than other RLT programs given the backcountry component and required technical gear.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Norway: Peaks and Valleys, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Students camp in tents for the entire trip on São Miguel Island, sharing tents in groups of 2-3, organized by gender. Showers available every 1-2 days; campsite bathrooms include clean, flush toilets and other facilities. The group works together to set up camp, prepare meals, and keep shared spaces clean throughout. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Azores: The Secret Island, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Accommodation shifts across three settings. 5 nights in simple hotels with beds and bathrooms in San José and on the Caribbean coast; 6 nights in a rustic house in Turrialba near the local community, working and living alongside host families (a shared-house, host-family-adjacent arrangement rather than a traditional one-family homestay); and 2 nights at riverside campsites on raised jungle platform tents in the rainforest. Teens share tents or rooms based on gender and comfort, with leaders close by; flush toilets and short daily showers are available throughout. Everyone helps set up tents, clean shared spaces, and pack up gear. No staff ratio stated; given this serves grades 6-8, families should expect age-appropriate guidance though specific supervision detail beyond the general description is not provided.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Costa Rica: Journey through the Jungle, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Unlike every other Road Less Traveled program researched, this one involves no tent camping at all. Twin rooms at clean, locally run hotels across Tokyo, Yamagata, and Tsuruoka (gender-shared, private bathrooms, AC and Wi-Fi). One night at a shukubo, a traditional pilgrim lodge historically used by mountain monks, sleeping on futons in tatami-mat rooms for a slower, more rustic pace. Most locations include laundry access and on-site staff for local recommendations. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Japan: Between Two Worlds, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Simple, locally owned hotels/guesthouses in Lima, Cusco, and Ollantaytambo (shared rooms, 2-3 per room, gender-divided), plus 3 nights of tent camping in a remote mountain village (tents for 2-3, mountain views, starry skies). Mix of western-style bathrooms and squat toilets depending on location; short showers every 1-2 days, more frequent in towns, less so while camping. No single rooms anywhere on this program; everyone shares space and pitches in. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Peru: Mystic Mountains, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Mix of rustic campsites and cozy yurts for 7 nights, plus a shared group house for 6 nights. During camping portions, teens share tents (2-3 per tent), divided by gender. Basic amenities with flush bathrooms; short showers typically every 1-3 days. Everyone pitches in to set up tents, cook meals, and keep shared spaces clean. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Alaska: Midnight Sun, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Tent camping throughout the trip at a mix of established campgrounds across Southern Iceland, shared tents (2-3 per tent), divided by gender. Simple but family-friendly campsites, rustic bathrooms, short showers typically every 2-3 days. Everyone helps set up camp, prep meals, keep shared spaces clean. No staff ratio stated. Given the wide grades 8-11 band, families should confirm how mixed-age grouping is handled day to day.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Iceland: Nordic Elements, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Accommodation shifts across three settings. In San José and on the Caribbean coast, the group stays in simple hotels with beds and bathrooms for 4 nights. In Turrialba, the group tent camps for 6 nights near the local community, working and living alongside host families. During a rafting adventure, the group sleeps at riverside campsites for 3 nights on platform tents in the rainforest, surrounded by the sounds of wildlife. Teens share tents or rooms based on gender and comfort, with leaders close by. Bathrooms range from hotel-style flush toilets to more rustic facilities depending on location; short showers are available every 1-2 days. Everyone helps with daily chores like setting up tents and keeping shared spaces clean, framed as building connection. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Costa Rica: Coast to Canopy, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Tent camping at coastal campsites/beaches for most of the trip, shared tents 2-4 per tent (wider than typical RLT capacity), gender-divided. Athens: 2 nights Airbnb-style home at start, 1 night hotel at end, both slumber-party style rooms. Toilets and short showers every 1-2 days. Everyone helps pitch tents, prep food, pack up camp. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Greece: Coastal Conservation, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Modest hotels throughout the entire 20-day trip -- no tent camping. Teens share rooms, gender-divided, leaders in separate nearby rooms. Western-style bathrooms, daily showers. Everyone helps tidy rooms and keep group spaces organized. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Thailand: Elephants, Education, and Cultural Exploration, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Single private, locally-owned Airbnb-style house throughout, no camping (explicitly stated). Cozy, communal, like a big group sleepover. Shared rooms hold 4-8 students each, gender-divided. A/C, flush bathrooms, showers every 1-2 days. Everyone helps keep shared spaces clean and organized. No staff ratio stated; given the 4-8 person rooms and grades 6-8 age band, confirm supervision detail directly.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Puerto Rico: Reefs to Rainforests, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Mix of campgrounds and group housing across Colorado and Wyoming. 9 nights tent camping near Kindness Ranch and in Rocky Mountain National Park, then 4 nights Airbnb-style group housing near Fort Collins. Shared tents/rooms gender-divided, rustic bathrooms, showers every 2-3 days. Group cooks, cleans, and keeps things running together. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Colorado: Tails of Kindness, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Private, locally-owned Airbnb-style housing throughout, no camping. Shared rooms, rotating beds/sleeping mats, gender-grouped, casual 'slumber party' feel. Bathrooms shared and basic, showers every 1-2 days, water conservation encouraged. Most meals shared on outdoor patios or in common kitchens. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Puerto Rico: Reef Restoration, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Camping in the Colorado wilderness for the full 14 days, no hotel/house component at any point. Shared tents, 2-3 per tent, gender-divided, all provided by RLT. Camp-style flush toilets, showers every 3-4 days. Teens help with meal prep, camp upkeep, group logistics. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Colorado: Call of the Wild, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Mix of rustic hotels, hostels, and small lodges throughout, no camping. Shared/slumber-party-style rooms, gender-divided. Lodges range from ensuite to shared facilities, quick showers every 2-3 days. Everyone helps with setup, gear organization, keeping spaces clean. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Scotland & Ireland: Celtic Isles, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Family-run hostel in Barcelona for 8 nights, then a mountain bunkhouse refuge for 4 nights, no camping. Shared rooms with 2-4 participants, gender-divided. Beds, bathrooms, A/C, not luxury. Showers typically every 1-2 days depending on itinerary. Each accommodation serves as a base to explore from, eat, and unwind together. No staff ratio stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots, Spain: Mountains to Mediterranean, Accommodations section

dayToDay.notes: Homestay-based. Visits to the European Parliament's Parlamentarium and the Hemicycle (where MEPs debate and vote), the Belgian Comic Art Museum, and a day trip to the medieval town of Dinant and the Caves of Han. Includes a hands-on chocolate-making workshop with a master chocolatier. Culminates in a student debate on a current global challenge.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: CIEE Diplomacy & Government (Brussels) program page

dayToDay.notes: Students live aboard a 45-50 ft monohull or catamaran full-time for the duration of the voyage, with 12 students and 3 staff per vessel (Skipper, first mate, and typically a third staff member such as a SCUBA instructor, medic, or marine biologist). Staff live aboard with students throughout. Each vessel has 5 cabins plus a large salon that converts to a 6th cabin, and 4 full bathrooms (heads); many students choose to sleep on deck under the stars in hammocks on clear nights. A rotating 'Job Wheel' assigns each student a different daily role (Skipper, Mate, Navigator, Engineer, Head Chef, plus support roles). Students prepare all meals themselves with staff help, using packaged/canned goods imported from the US plus fresh produce picked up locally roughly every 4 days; vegetarian, vegan, and common allergy accommodations are available with advance notice. Nova sails alongside the wider ActionQuest fleet (6-8 vessels) as a 'flotilla,' meeting the larger group at signature moments like beach BBQs. This day-to-day structure (staffing ratio, Job Wheel, Forum discussions, food policy, flotilla sailing) is standard across the ActionQuest British Virgin Islands fleet, not unique to Nova.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest Nova program page, Accommodations, Food, and Group Living FAQ sections (org-wide fleet policy)

dayToDay.notes: Same live-aboard structure as the rest of the ActionQuest BVI fleet: 45-50 ft monohull or catamaran, roughly 12 students and 3 staff per vessel, rotating Job Wheel roles, student-prepared meals, and flotilla sailing alongside other AQ vessels with shared beach BBQs and events.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest org-wide fleet policy, cross-referenced from the Nova and Vega program pages

dayToDay.notes: Unlike the BVI live-aboard fleet, this program is a mixed land-and-sea itinerary in Australia: students stay in a mix of shore-based accommodations and time aboard a yacht sailing the Whitsunday Islands, with a group size of roughly 10-14 students and 2 staff (smaller than the typical BVI vessel of 12 students/3 staff). Includes hands-on community service work with the Daintree Observatory rainforest replanting project. Run in conjunction with ActionQuest's sister program GoBeyond, which may mean shared staffing or logistics with that program's structure.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest Reef to Rainforest program page (Australia)

dayToDay.notes: Lives aboard a 50-ft monohull or 46-ft catamaran with a smaller-than-typical group: 10 students and 2 staff per vessel, sailing in a small flotilla of just 1-2 vessels (versus the main BVI fleet's 6-8 vessels) for most of the voyage, though it begins and ends alongside the larger BVI fleet. The itinerary spans over 10 islands from the BVI to Antigua and back, so days involve more open-water passages and changing customs/currencies/languages than the more geographically contained BVI-only programs.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest Minerva program page (Caribbean Leeward Islands)

dayToDay.notes: Lives aboard a 46-foot catamaran. Days are heavily scuba-focused given the 25-dive curriculum, working through PADI Advanced Open Water and 5 specialty topics at dive sites including Alice's Wonderland, Blue Chromis Reef, and the wreck of the Chikuzen. Otherwise follows the standard ActionQuest fleet structure (Job Wheel, student-prepared meals, flotilla sailing).
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest Neptune program page (British Virgin Islands)

dayToDay.notes: Standard ActionQuest BVI fleet structure, with days built around the marine biology curriculum: 20-22 dives working toward the AQ Tropical Marine Biology Course, Research Diver Distinctive Specialty, and additional PADI specialties like Underwater Photography and Underwater Naturalist.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest Dolphin program page (British Virgin Islands)

dayToDay.notes: Standard ActionQuest BVI fleet structure, with an advanced sailing emphasis: the vessel circumnavigates the entire BVI, giving students more time at the helm plotting courses and standing watch than on the intro-level programs, alongside advanced scuba diving at sites like Mountain Point, The Chimneys, Spy Glass, and Coral Gardens.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest Carina program page (British Virgin Islands)

dayToDay.notes: Standard ActionQuest BVI fleet structure, balancing 10 advanced dives (PADI Advanced Open Water plus Peak Performance Buoyancy) with an intro-level sailing curriculum for students newer to sailing.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest Aquarius program page (British Virgin Islands)

dayToDay.notes: Standard ActionQuest BVI fleet structure, with days weighted toward advanced sailing (keelboat handling, small dinghy practice, IYT International Crew & VHF Radio training) alongside an introductory scuba diving curriculum for students new to diving.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest Polaris program page (British Virgin Islands)

dayToDay.notes: Standard ActionQuest BVI fleet structure, but with a younger student cohort (ages 14 and under) than every other ActionQuest program researched. Days combine 14-18 dives working toward PADI Junior Advanced Open Water and specialties like Project AWARE and Underwater Naturalist. Given the younger age range, families should ask directly about any additional supervision adjustments beyond the standard 12-students/3-staff ratio.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest Barracuda program page (British Virgin Islands)

dayToDay.notes: Slightly larger vessel groups than the standard ActionQuest ratio: 13 students and 3 staff per vessel, across a flotilla of 3-4 vessels that shares a basic itinerary with the Dolphin and Neptune programs. Days center on PADI Rescue Diver training and rescue-scenario practice, including helping guide Neptune students through rescue drills as an introduction to Divemaster-level responsibility.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest Rescue program page (British Virgin Islands)

dayToDay.notes: Standard ActionQuest BVI fleet structure, but structured as a professional internship: students take on more instructional and mentorship responsibility as part of PADI Junior Divemaster training, working through 20+ dives.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest Junior Divemaster program page (British Virgin Islands)

dayToDay.notes: Standard ActionQuest BVI fleet structure, but for the oldest and most advanced cohort (18+, already PADI Rescue Divers with 40+ logged dives): students take on the most professional-level responsibility of any ActionQuest program, working toward PADI Professional Divemaster certification.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: ActionQuest Professional Divemaster program page (British Virgin Islands)

dayToDay.notes: Students live with a host family (homestay) in Shanghai for the duration of the program, with three meals a day provided and dietary needs accommodated. All ground transportation once in-country is included, along with all cultural activities and excursions and interactive classes. Wi-Fi access is available at accommodations, but no international data plan or SIM card is included, so students should plan connectivity separately for time outside housing. Pre-departure advice and orientation are provided before travel, and CIEE provides 24/7 emergency on-site support plus comprehensive medical and travel protection (iNext Travel Insurance) throughout the program. An optional flight chaperone is available (flight cost itself is not included in tuition). As with other CIEE China programs, families should note that China maintains strict regulations on medications brought into the country, and are encouraged to consult a doctor and confirm any of the student's medications are legal and available in China before departure.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: CIEE Art History & Chinese Culture (Shanghai) program page, What's Included and Eligibility sections

dayToDay.notes: Students split their 4 weeks between two settings. On campus in Leadville, Colorado, they live in cabins as part of a residential community, participating in writing workshops or ecology research, plus rock climbing at nearby crags and whitewater rafting on the Arkansas River. During the two 10-day backpacking expeditions, students travel in small expedition groups of 8-10 students, led by experienced HMI wilderness instructors who teach technical and wilderness travel skills; each group forms a tight-knit community over the course of the trip, and all students get the chance to take on leadership roles. The page does not detail a specific staff-to-student ratio for either the campus or expedition portions, nor describe cabin room-sharing arrangements or bathroom/shower facilities in the level of detail seen on some other providers' pages.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: High Mountain Institute Summer Term program page, main description and Why HMI Summer Term stats sections

dayToDay.notes: Students travel in a single small group of 12 students and 3 instructors for the full 4 weeks, so this ratio (roughly 4:1) holds throughout every phase of the program rather than varying by activity. Accommodation type shifts by week: several nights in a workshop/orientation setting in Candelaria near Sucre; homestays with a Quechua farming family in Tiquipaya (near Cochabamba) for 1-2 weeks with few amenities described as part of the program's 'Rugged Travel' component; multi-day backcountry camping during both the Cordillera de los Frailes trek (week 2, 4 days) and the student-led Expedition Phase trek (week 4, 5 days, descending from the high Andes into cloud forest); and a final stay at an eco-lodge in Coroico. The program explicitly rates 'Rugged Travel' as a defining component, describing homestays with few amenities, extensive high-altitude walking, and lengthy public transportation travel. In week 4, students take on increased ownership over trip planning and logistics as part of the 'Expedition Phase,' a deliberate hand-off of responsibility rather than staff running the entire itinerary throughout.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons Bolivia: Spanish Language Immersion in the Andes program page, Group Size, Program Components, and Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors travel together throughout. Accommodation shifts through several homestays: a short homestay with Kiche Maya families in Pachaj, an extended homestay in San Juan la Laguna on Lake Atitlan, another homestay in the traditional Maya community of Todos Santos, and a final homestay/fieldwork stay in San Juan Cotzal working alongside a weaving cooperative of civil-war widows. A 3-day trek from Quetzaltenango to Lake Atitlan involves camping/trail lodging between homestays. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors. Days split between lodges/guesthouses during a short ridge trek out of Bhaktapur, a rural village homestay (10+ days total across rural and urban placements) with subsistence-farming families, a short stay at a Tibetan Buddhist monastery for a meditation retreat, and an urban homestay in Patan with Newari host families. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors. Begins in a hillside town (Jiufen) for group-culture building, then a multi-night rural homestay with organic-farming families in Yilan County, and a final city stretch in Taipei. Rugged Travel is explicitly rated low given Taiwan's developed infrastructure (train, bus, bicycle). No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors. Unlike most other WTBD programs, this one explicitly does NOT include individual homestays; instead the group stays in community housing throughout Bhutan (Thimpu, Punakha, Paro) and starts/ends with a hotel/inn stay in Kathmandu, Nepal. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors, matching the standard WTBD group size. The provided screenshots confirm this ratio and the program description (Andes trekking, Machu Picchu, Amazon River basin) but do not include the detailed week-by-week itinerary, program components ratings, or specific homestay/accommodation breakdown seen on other WTBD programs researched via direct page fetch. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size, and no accommodation-type detail, could be confirmed from the material available.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: User-provided screenshots of the Where There Be Dragons Peru: Sacred Mountains program page, At a Glance section

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors (same group size as the 4-week sibling program). Shorter homestay stretch: an orientation stay at a coffee farm, a brief homestay with Kiche Maya families in Pachaj, and an extended homestay in San Juan la Laguna on Lake Atitlan, connected by a 3-day trek from Quetzaltenango. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors. Days move through a natural-park orientation stay in Los Alcornocales (Cadiz), a village stay in El Borge (Axarquia region) with local raisin-farming families, a homestay (or alternative accommodation, per the page) in Huetor Vega outside Granada for the bulk of the reforestation/climate work, and a final comfortable group lodging in Malaga for the last two nights. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors. Begins with a local inn stay in Wakayama for orientation, moves to a 3-7 day homestay in coastal Kyotango (students may be individually placed or paired with another Dragons student depending on the community), then Kyoto for Independent Study Projects including a supervised student-led group excursion, and closes with sightseeing days in Tokyo. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors. Accommodation spans three distinct settings: an urban/semi-urban homestay in Yogyakarta, a mountain stay near the Dieng Plateau, and finally living directly with the Bajau 'sea nomad' community in stilted homes over open water in Wakatobi. The Rugged Travel component explicitly notes some students sleep on bamboo mats on the floor in certain homestays, under the stars on beaches, and in group jungle camping. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors. Opens with a stay at a small family-owned guesthouse near a remote, un-renovated section of the Great Wall, then Beijing city exploration, then an extended (5+ day) rural homestay with a Naxi ethnic-minority community in Lashihai near Lijiang, and finally an extended urban homestay in Kunming with classes held at a dedicated 'Program House' near Green Lake Park. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors. Begins with an orientation site near Leh for altitude acclimatization, then homestays in small Ladakhi villages during the shorter Sham Valley trek, then tent camping during the second, more challenging extended trek (supported by a team of guides, cooks, and pack ponies), with an exchange stop at the SECMOL sustainable-education campus. Closes with city time in Leh and a day in Delhi. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors. Starts in a local guesthouse in Phnom Penh for orientation, continues through Battambang and Siem Reap (hotel/guesthouse style lodging), a short silent retreat at a meditation center, an extended rural homestay in Banteay Chhmar with a Khmer farming community as the core of the program, and closes in Kampot where students organize their own transport and activities as part of a supervised 'Expedition Phase.' No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors. Moves through an orientation stay in Sukhothai, a 3-day stay at a Buddhist monastery for a meditation retreat, a 5-day homestay with Karen community families in Huai Hin Lad Nai, a stay at Earth Home (a sustainable-living center), and a final student-led 2-day expedition phase in Chiang Rai (with instructor oversight) before closing in the mountains of Chiang Dao. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors. Begins with an orientation stay in a small Middle Atlas Mountains town, then a 4-5 day semi-urban homestay in Azrou with Berber (Amazigh) families, city exploration in Fez (staying near the medina), and a closing multi-day trek with camping in the High Atlas Mountains through remote villages and nomadic communities. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: 12 students and 3 instructors. Days spent in a seaside community inside a national park near St. Louis (day-stays with local families for meals), then a stop in Touba, and a multi-day homestay in Thies with local families for the bulk of the program, including a day trip to Dakar. Closes on the cliffside beaches of Toubab Dialaw for a group Transference Phase. No specific staff-to-student ratio beyond the 12:3 group size is stated.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: Where There Be Dragons program page, Group Size and Program Components/Itinerary Example sections

dayToDay.notes: Six campuses (3 boys, 3 girls), subdivided into cabin groups by grade. Wake-up 7:45am (older campuses) or 8:10am (younger); bedtime 8:30pm-11:00pm scaling with age. Typical day: wake-up/breakfast, morning 'Cove' gathering, cabin clean-up, 3 morning activities, buffet lunch, rest hour, 2 afternoon activities, all-camp 6th period (free choice for older campers, shower/down-time for younger), dinner, evening Cove, evening cabin program, bedtime. Two seatings for breakfast/dinner; whole camp eats lunch together. 3:1+ camper-to-staff ratio; counselors mostly college students/teachers, most over 20. Younger campers have required activities (swim/tennis lessons, team sports); older campers build individualized schedules and can specialize. All cabins have electricity and overnight night-lights.

dayToDay.notes: Residential students live in dorms on the host university campus for the full 8 days, with an Advisor and classroom group assigned on Day 1 alongside icebreaker activities. dayToDay.notes: Students must hold PADI Open Water certification or equivalent to enroll. Maximum dive depth is 60ft for standard certified divers and up to 80-90ft for the most advanced students; divers aged 11 are capped at 40ft and must dive with a PADI professional or certified diver; ages 12-14 with additional Junior Advanced Open Water training may go to 70ft. Equipment is rinsed in freshwater after every dive per PADI-recommended practice. dayToDay.notes: The program begins with a full-group gathering at base camp (an island on a lake in Temagami) where staff and all participants discuss the community they're forming and agree on shared values (honesty, acceptance, trust, patience, humour). The first few days are spent building backcountry travel skills with staff and more experienced participants: portaging, packing a Duluth bag and wannigan, setting up a tent, and paddling technique. Once the group is acquainted, participants are divided into 'sections' of 6-12 participants led by 2-3 staff, formed according to individual needs, skill level, and group dynamics -- these sections then embark on their own canoe-tripping route, ranging from local lake/stream excursions near base camp to more challenging whitewater river expeditions, depending on the section's experience and skill. Leaders draw on training and experience to guide each group through the trip, building trust, communication, and community as the section sets goals, solves problems together, and makes decisions collectively. All sections return to base camp on the same day, arriving within minutes of each other to a staff-and-director welcome on the docks, followed by a shared feast and storytelling in the dining hall. The next day is spent re-integrating into the larger camp community: de-outfitting canoe trip gear, doing 'giveaways,' and a ceremony honoring each participant's accomplishments and contributions. The following day, participants from the brother program Langskib (for boys/young men) arrive by Voyageur canoe for a joint barbecue and celebration, where sections from both programs share stories from the trail.

dayToDay.notes: Students live in upscale student apartments in central Seville, controlled by World Class Programs and shared only with other World Class students (no host families). Apartments have living rooms, kitchens, bathrooms, and 2-3 bedrooms, each shared by two students; staff are housed in a separate apartment down the hall from students. A dedicated Security Officer stays in the building, on-call to students 24/7. Weekday structure: major class (Spanish History, Fine Art & Drawing, or Spanish Language at Beginner or Advanced/Immersion level) meets every weekday morning; minor/elective class meets three afternoons a week (Monday, Wednesday, Friday). On non-minor-class afternoons, students join a group activity. Weekends are used for day trips to other Spanish cities (Madrid, Cordoba, Gibraltar). Free time is available for the city's cafe scene and shopping districts "within safety guidelines."
dayToDay.sourceCitation: World Class Programs Spain program page

dayToDay.notes: Students live with other World Class Programs students in shared accommodations within walking distance of the host city's major landmarks -- described explicitly as a "pre-college dorm life experience," with no homestays. Accommodations include washing machines and air conditioning; staff are housed separately in the same building, with a dedicated Security Officer on-call 24/7 when the program is large enough. Weekday structure: major class (Classical History & Archaeology, Fine Art & Drawing, or Western Religion & Traditions) meets every weekday morning; minor class (Western Philosophy, Digital Photography, or Mediterranean Cuisine) meets three afternoons a week, with a group activity on the other afternoons. Day trips throughout the 3 weeks take students to sites across Greece and southern Italy (planned visits, subject to change year to year, have included Santorini, Mykonos, Crete, the Ruins of Ephesus, the Amalfi Coast/Positano, and Pompeii) rather than being confined to weekends only, since this program spans two countries.
dayToDay.sourceCitation: World Class Programs Greece (Greece & Italy: Western Civilization) program page

dayToDay.notes: Students live in upscale student apartments or hotels in central Osaka, controlled by World Class Programs and shared only with other World Class students. Each bedroom is shared by 2-4 students, with staff housed in a fully separate accommodation in the same location; a dedicated Security Officer stays on-call 24/7 when the program is large enough. Weekday structure: major class (Japanese History, Japanese Language, or Manga Creation) meets every weekday morning; minor class (Philosophy, Photography, or Japanese Cuisine) meets three afternoons a week. Students take weekly excursions to other Japanese cities, including Tokyo and Kyoto.
